about: Curated reference records: the basic numbers of the three gravity environments the database covers (Moon, Mars, 0 g) and how designs change with gravity. Values are rounded reference values; the comparison numbers are computed from g with the stated formulas.

records.title: Moon: surface gravity and environment reference values
records.summary: Gravity on the lunar surface is 1.62 m/s^2, about one sixth of Earth's (0.165 g). The Moon has no real atmosphere, a day-night cycle of 29.5 Earth days (so about two weeks of darkness away from the poles) and surface temperatures that swing by roughly 300 K at the equator.
records.details: What this means for a habitat: weight loads are about six times smaller than on Earth while internal pressure loads are unchanged, so the pressure hull, not the weight, sizes the structure. The two-week night drives energy storage (or nuclear power, or polar sites with near-continuous light). With no atmosphere there is no convective cooling outside, no aerodynamic braking for landers, and no protection from radiation or micrometeoroids. The gravity field is lumpy (mass concentrations, 'mascons', under the large basins), which perturbs low lunar orbits.

facts.name: day-night cycle (synodic period)
facts.note: about 14.8 days of light then 14.8 days of dark at the equator

records.title: Mars: surface gravity and environment reference values
records.summary: Gravity on the surface of Mars is 3.71 m/s^2, about 38% of Earth's (0.378 g). A Martian day (sol) is 24 h 39.6 min, the year is 687 Earth days, and the atmosphere is thin carbon dioxide at well under 1% of Earth's sea-level pressure.
records.details: What this means for a habitat: weight loads are about 2.6 times smaller than on Earth; internal pressure still dominates the hull. The atmosphere is too thin to breathe or to stop radiation well, but thick enough to matter: it gives some aerodynamic braking for landing, carries dust (storms reduce solar power), allows convective heat loss, and is a carbon-dioxide resource for making oxygen and propellant. Sunlight is on average about 43% as strong as at Earth. The near-24-hour day keeps night storage needs similar to Earth. Communication with Earth is delayed by minutes, so operations must be autonomous.

records.title: 0 g: what microgravity (weightlessness) actually is
records.summary: Weightlessness in orbit is free fall, not the absence of gravity: at the International Space Station's altitude (about 400 km) gravity is still about 8.7 m/s^2, roughly 89% of the surface value. Station and crew fall around the Earth together, so nothing presses on anything. The small accelerations that remain are around a millionth of g, hence 'microgravity'.
records.details: Ways to get 0 g, shortest to longest: drop towers (seconds), parabolic aircraft flights (about 20-25 seconds per parabola), sounding rockets (minutes), and orbit (months). What changes when weight disappears: no buoyant convection (flames become spherical and slow, hot air does not rise, so forced ventilation is needed for cooling and to stop carbon dioxide pockets), no sedimentation, liquids are ruled by surface tension (tanks need capillary devices, boiling is harder to control), and the human body unloads (bone and muscle loss, fluid shift toward the head), which is why crews exercise about two hours a day.

facts.name: typical residual acceleration on a space station

records.title: Earth, Mars, Moon and 0 g compared: how things scale with gravity
records.summary: Surface gravity: Earth 9.81 m/s^2 (1 g), Mars 3.71 m/s^2 (0.378 g), Moon 1.62 m/s^2 (0.165 g), orbit about 0 g. Anything driven by weight scales with g; anything driven by pressure, inertia or surface tension does not.
records.details: Scales directly with g: weight of a mass (m x g), hydrostatic pressure in a liquid (rho x g x h), structural loads from self-weight, traction available to a rover (so drawbar pull and climbing ability drop). Scales with 1/g: how far a thrown or ejected object travels (dust and rocket-plume ejecta fly 2.6 times farther on Mars and 6 times farther on the Moon, before counting the missing air drag). Scales with 1/sqrt(g): time to fall a given height (t = sqrt(2h/g)) and the period of a pendulum or a walking leg, which is why people move slowly and tend to hop on the Moon. Buoyant convection (hot air rising, flames stretching upward) weakens as g drops and vanishes at 0 g. Unchanged by gravity: mass and inertia (a heavy crate is as hard to start and stop as on Earth), internal pressure loads on a hull (sigma = P x r / t), surface tension and capillary forces, radiation and thermal radiation.
